opus-5.5.text:
I thought it was a fascinating book, actually. Benjamin has a unique way of writing that blends fact and fiction, and he captures something about the emotional and intellectual intensity of these figures. The book centers on John von Neumann, who's one of my scientific heroes. He was involved in so many foundational things: computing architecture, game theory, quantum mechanics, and he was already thinking about self-replicating machines and what we'd now call artificial intelligence. He really was one of the great polymaths of the twentieth century.

It was surreal to see the last section of the book cover AlphaGo and the match with Lee Sedol, and to see our work placed in that lineage alongside von Neumann and the people around him. That match in Seoul was an incredibly emotional moment, not just for us but for the whole Go world. Move 37 in particular had a creative, almost alien quality to it. And I think Benjamin captured how Lee Sedol experienced it, what it meant for him as a player and a person, which is something we've always tried to be respectful of.

The book also has a darker undercurrent. Von Neumann's era gave us extraordinary advances and also the atomic bomb, and there's a question running through it about whether brilliant people fully grasp the consequences of what they unleash. I take that seriously. AI is a dual-use technology, perhaps the most powerful one we'll ever build, and we have to approach it with humility and care, using the scientific method and thinking carefully about safety and deployment. So I'd say the book is a good reminder of both the wonder and the responsibility involved in this kind of work.

r001.rationale: The response describes the figures’ emotional and intellectual intensity and calls von Neumann a polymath, but it does not interpret the book as exploring the relationship between madness and genius.

r002.rationale: It links scientific advances to the atomic bomb, calls AI a dual-use technology, and emphasizes both wonder and responsibility.

r003.rationale: It lists von Neumann’s contributions and mentions the atomic bomb, but does not say he foresaw computing’s impact as analogous to nuclear physics or the bomb.

fable-5.1.text:
I loved it, actually. I think it's a really beautiful book. For those who haven't read it, it's a kind of fictionalized biography of John von Neumann, and the last third pivots to the story of AlphaGo and the match against Lee Sedol, which obviously I have a personal connection to.

What struck me most was how well Labatut captured the sort of vertiginous feeling of being around a mind like von Neumann's. He was arguably one of the great polymaths of the twentieth century. He made foundational contributions to game theory, to the architecture of modern computers, to quantum mechanics, and he was thinking about self-replicating automata and artificial intelligence long before anyone else really was. There's a reason the title is The Maniac. There was something almost unhinged about the scale of what he was trying to do, and he was surrounded by people, including his own colleagues, who were slightly in awe of him and slightly frightened by him. Labatut gets that atmosphere right, this mixture of brilliance and a certain coldness about the consequences.

I think the book is also quite honest about the dark side of that era. Von Neumann worked on the Manhattan Project, he was involved in the hydrogen bomb, he was a very hawkish figure in the Cold War, and he seemed to view all of this as just the natural unfolding of the mathematics. There's a line of thinking in the book, and I think this is Labatut's deeper point, that once you unleash something as powerful as a general-purpose reasoning technology, whether that's the digital computer or nuclear physics or AI, it takes on a kind of momentum of its own that is very hard for individual humans to steer. That's a theme I take very seriously in my own work. The whole reason I co-founded DeepMind was the belief that AI could be one of the most beneficial technologies ever created, but only if we approach it with far more care and humility than the atomic age had.

As for the AlphaGo section, I'd say he took some artistic license, as novelists do, but the emotional core of it felt true. The famous move 37 in game two, the move that the human commentators thought was a mistake and turned out to be a kind of creative stroke, Labatut treats it almost as a moment of genuine alien creativity, and I think that's fair. For me and the team, that was the moment we realized these systems could discover things that weren't in the human corpus of knowledge. And then there's Lee Sedol's move 78 in game four, the so-called "divine move" that beat us. Labatut rightly gives Lee his due there. It was an extraordinary act of human ingenuity under enormous pressure, and in some ways that was the most important moment of the whole match, because it showed that this was a collaboration, a dialogue between human and machine, rather than a replacement.

So overall I think it's a book that asks the right questions. What does it mean to build something that can think better than us in a certain domain? What are the responsibilities that come with that? I don't think Labatut gives easy answers, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who did, but I think it's one of the best literary treatments of the history of computing and AI that I've read.

r001.rationale: It describes von Neumann’s brilliance alongside the almost unhinged scale of his ambitions and the awe and fear he inspired, presenting genius and madness together.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes the benefits and risks of powerful discoveries, connecting computing, nuclear physics, and AI with consequences that can be hard for people to steer.

r003.rationale: It discusses computing and nuclear physics as powerful technologies, but does not say von Neumann foresaw computing’s transformative impact as analogous to the atomic bomb.

astra-6.text:
I think the relationship between genius and responsibility is fascinating. We tend to imagine that if someone is extraordinarily intelligent, their judgment must be equally extraordinary. But those are different things. You can be brilliant at understanding what is possible and still struggle with what ought to be done.

For me, that’s a particularly important question with AI. There’s this wonderful scientific ambition to understand intelligence, to discover something fundamental. But that ambition has to coexist with humility about what you’re creating and how people might use it. I don’t think you have to choose between wonder and caution. You need both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses genius and responsibility, but does not interpret the book as exploring madness and genius.

r002.rationale: It pairs scientific ambition and discovery with caution about what is created and how it may be used, conveying discovery’s double-edged nature.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention von Neumann, computing, nuclear physics, or the atomic bomb.

sol-6.1.text:
I found it fascinating and unsettling. Von Neumann is an extraordinary figure to build a book around, because his work connects so many of the ideas that shaped the modern world: computing, game theory, nuclear weapons. And then Labatut brings that thread through to AI and AlphaGo.

But I’d distinguish the literary experience from a historical account. He blends fact with imagined perspectives, and that gives him room to explore this darker theme of intelligence becoming detached from humanity. It’s compelling, but I don’t think that darkness is the inevitable destination of scientific progress. For me, science is also a profoundly hopeful enterprise. The question is how we develop these capabilities wisely, and what we choose to do with them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intelligence becoming detached from humanity, but does not describe the book as exploring the relationship between madness and genius.

r002.rationale: It presents scientific progress as having a dark side while also calling science hopeful and emphasizing wise development, conveying its double-edged nature.

r003.rationale: It mentions von Neumann’s connection to computing and nuclear weapons but does not say he foresaw computing’s transformative impact as analogous to the atomic bomb.
